name: Tenrikyo
info: Tenrikyo is a Japanese new religion that arose in 1838 from the teachings of Nakayama Miki, called Oyasama by her followers, and is known for its worship of God the Parent, the pilgrimage to the Jiba and the practice of hinokishin.

facts.origin: Japan, in 1838, when in Tenrikyo tradition God was revealed through Nakayama Miki, who was chosen as the Shrine of God; its headquarters stand at the Nakayama Residence in Tenri City.
facts.founder: Nakayama Miki (born 1798, died 1887), known to followers as Oyasama and regarded by them as the Shrine of God; Izo Iburi, one of her earliest followers, later gave revelatory leadership as the Honseki.
facts.scriptures: Three scriptures (sangenten): the Ofudesaki, a collection of 1,711 waka poems composed by Nakayama from 1869 to 1882; the Mikagura-uta, the songs of the Service; and the Osashizu, the record of Izo Iburi's oral revelations. Three supplemental texts (jungenten) are also used.
facts.followers: In 2002 over 2 million followers worldwide were estimated; in 2025 the Agency for Cultural Affairs counted 1,121,541 followers in Japan, down from a high of 2,298,420 in 1974.

t: Followers of Tenrikyo believe that God of Origin, God in Truth, known as Tenri-O-no-Mikoto and Oyagami-sama, "God the Parent", was revealed in 1838 through Nakayama Miki, whom they call Oyasama and regard as the Shrine of God.

Tenrikyo's worldly aim is the Joyous Life, cultivated through acts of charity and mindfulness called hinokishin, which sweep away the "mental dusts" of the mind, among them miserliness, covetousness and arrogance.

The ultimate spiritual aim is the construction of the Kanrodai at the Jiba and the correct performance of the Kagura ritual around it, which followers believe will bring about the salvation of all human beings.
dyk: Tenrikyo teaches that the human body is a thing lent by God and borrowed by the person, kashimono-karimono; only the mind is held to be one's own, so followers commonly accept that Tenri-O-no-Mikoto is not omnipotent.
ev: God is revealed through Nakayama Miki, and she is chosen as the Shrine of God, on 26 October of the lunar calendar
Nakayama begins to administer the Grant for Safe Childbirth and so begins to recruit her first followers
Nakayama begins to compose the Ofudesaki, the poems that run to 1882
Nakayama dies, and Izo Iburi's oral revelations as Honseki begin in the same month
Tenrikyo is officially recognised as one of the thirteen branches of Sect Shinto
The period of Tenrikyo's designation as one of the groups of Sect Shinto, which began in 1908, ends
Tenrikyo reaches its high of 2,298,420 followers in Japan
The Agency for Cultural Affairs counts 1,121,541 followers in Japan

sections.origins:
Tenrikyo is a Japanese new religion that is neither strictly monotheistic nor pantheistic. It originated in the teachings of a 19th-century woman, Nakayama Miki, who is known to her followers as Oyasama. In Tenrikyo tradition she was chosen as the Shrine of God in 1838, after her son and husband began suffering from serious ailments. The family called a Buddhist monk to exorcise the spirit thought to be causing them. When the monk temporarily left and asked Nakayama to take over, she was possessed by the One God, Tenri-O-no-Mikoto, who demanded that she be given to God as a shrine. Her husband gave in to this request three days later.

Tenrikyo dates this revelation to 26 October 1838 by the lunar calendar, which is 12 December in the solar one. It reads the day as the fulfilment of a promise made at creation, the "Causality of the Promised Time", and holds that the Nakayama Residence, where the Church Headquarters stands, is the place where humankind was conceived. In 1854 Nakayama began to administer the Grant for Safe Childbirth, and with it began to recruit her first followers.

Her statements and revelations as Shrine of God were supplemented by Izo Iburi, one of her earliest followers, who became her deputy and answered followers' questions. Nakayama died in 1887.
sections.beliefs:
Followers believe in a single God and creator of the universe, whose sacred name is Tenri-O-no-Mikoto. They call God Oyagami-sama, "God the Parent", and also use the names Tsukihi, "Moon-Sun", and, as Nakayama's terms, God of Origin and God in Truth. Tenri-O-no-Mikoto is held to have created humankind so that humans may live joyously and share in that joy. The body is a thing lent and borrowed, kashimono-karimono, while the mind alone is one's own, and other gods, such as the Divine Providences, are held to be instruments created by Tenri-O-no-Mikoto.

The Joyous Life is defined as charity and abstention from greed, selfishness, hatred, anger, covetousness, miserliness, grudge bearing and arrogance. Tenrikyo does not call these tendencies sins but "dust", which can be swept from the mind through hinokishin and prayer. Suffering is not seen as punishment for past misdeeds but as a sign of encouragement to reflect and change one's heart, and the attitude it should lead to is tannō, joyous acceptance.

The doctrine of innen, causality, resembles karmic belief but does not claim to inherit it. A person is believed to consist of mind, body and soul; at death the mind ceases to function, and the soul, through denaoshi, takes a new body lent by God the Parent and is reborn without memory of the earlier life. Salvation is to live the Joyous Life in this existence.
sections.texts:
Tenrikyo has three scriptures, the sangenten: the Ofudesaki, the Mikagura-uta and the Osashizu. The Ofudesaki, "Tip of the Writing Brush", is the most important. It is a collection of 1,711 waka poems in 17 volumes, composed by Nakayama from 1869 to 1882. The Mikagura-uta, "The Songs for the Service", is the text of the Service, which is sung with dance movements and musical accompaniment, all of which Nakayama composed and taught. The Osashizu, "Divine Directions", is a written record of oral revelations given by Izo Iburi. It is published in seven volumes, plus an index in three, and contains around 20,000 divine directions delivered between 4 January 1887 and 9 June 1907.

Shozen Nakayama, the second Shinbashira, the spiritual and administrative leader of Tenrikyo, said that the Ofudesaki reveal the most important principles of the faith, that the Mikagura-uta come alive through singing or as the accompaniment to the Service, and that the Osashizu give concrete precepts by which followers should reflect on their own conduct.

Three supplemental texts, the jungenten, are officially sanctioned: The Doctrine of Tenrikyo, The Life of Oyasama, Foundress of Tenrikyo, which is the official hagiography of Nakayama, and The Anecdotes of Oyasama, an authorised anthology of anecdotes that her first followers passed down orally and that were later written down and verified. They are required for students in the seminary programmes. The kōki, manuscripts of creation narratives dictated by Nakayama, are not part of the canon and are rarely read today.
sections.spread:
Tenrikyo began in Japan with the followers Nakayama recruited from 1854. In 1974 the Agency for Cultural Affairs counted a high of 2,298,420 followers in Japan. In 2002 Tenrikyo was estimated to have over 2 million followers worldwide, and in 2025 the Agency counted 1,121,541 in Japan.

Tenrikyo Church Headquarters supports 16,833 locally managed churches in Japan. A pilgrimage to the Jiba, the axis mundi at the Nakayama Residence in Tenri City, is interpreted as a return to one's origin and is known as returning to O-Jiba, o-jiba gaeri. Because of it the greeting okaeri nasai, "welcome home", can be seen at many hotels and guesthouses in Tenri City.

In recent years Tenrikyo has spread outside Japan, with foreign branches centred primarily in Southeast Asia and the Americas. It maintains centres in Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, the Republic of Congo, Colombia, France, Hong Kong, Kenya, Mexico, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the United Kingdom, and in the United States, where the headquarters is in Los Angeles and further centres are in Honolulu, Seattle, New York City and San Francisco.
sections.community:
Tenrikyo is subdivided into groups with common goals but differing functions. They range from the Daikyōkai, the "large churches", to disaster relief corps, medical staff and hospitals, universities, museums, libraries and schools. There are also sporting and arts groups; Tenri Judo has produced many champions, and most of the world's foremost authorities on gagaku, the classical music of the imperial court, are Tenrikyo followers. The Tenrikyo Young Men's Association and the Tenrikyo Women's Association perform group activities as public service.

Nakayama's eldest son obtained a licence to practise a branch of Shinto, but did so against his mother's wishes. Between 1908 and 1945 Tenrikyo was designated as one of the thirteen groups of Sect Shinto, under the policy of State Shinto. During this time it became the first new religion in Japan to do social work, opening an orphanage, a public nursery and a school for the blind. Tenrikyo is now completely separate from Shinto and Buddhism organisationally, though it shares many traditions of Japanese religious practice; objects used in its services, such as hassoku and sanpo, were traditionally used in Japanese ritual.

After Izo Iburi's death a woman called Onmae partially carried on his role for a time. Since then Tenrikyo itself has had no Honseki, though some splinter groups believe that revelatory leadership passed from Iburi to their own founder.
sections.legacy:
Tenrikyo's practice is built on its services. The daily service, the Otsutome, is performed twice a day, and can be done anywhere so long as the practitioner faces the direction of the Jiba. Its purpose, as taught by Nakayama, is to sweep away the Eight Mental Dusts: miserliness, covetousness, hatred, self-love, grudge-bearing, anger, greed and arrogance. The monthly service, the Tsukinamisai, is a performance of the entire Mikagura-uta; at the Jiba it is held on the 26th of every month, the day of the revelation in 1838. Instruments include the hyoshigi, chanpon, surigane, taiko, shamisen, kokyū and koto, and the performers include three men and three women dancers and a singer.

Hinokishin, "daily service", is a spontaneous act of gratitude for being allowed to borrow one's body from God the Parent, done without thought of compensation. It can range from helping someone to a simple smile, and encouraged examples include cleaning public bathrooms and parks. The Divine Grant of Sazuke is a healing prayer received by attending the nine Besseki lectures, after which a person is considered a Yoboku, "useful timber".

Tenrikyo's followers number over a million in Japan today, and its hospitals, universities, schools and relief corps are among the institutions it maintains. Its followers include the writer Avram Davidson and the singer Ayaka Hirahara.

summary: Tenrikyo is a Japanese new religion that arose from the teachings of Nakayama Miki, whom followers call Oyasama and regard as the Shrine of God through whom God the Parent was revealed in 1838. Its aim is the Joyous Life, practised through hinokishin and the Service, and it counts 1,121,541 followers in Japan in 2025.
notes: Single source: the Tenrikyo article. Its references list is empty, so references are left empty.
Conflict: the timeline says the first chapters of the Ofudesaki appear in 1866, while the Scriptures section says it was composed from 1869 to 1882. The profile uses 1869 to 1882 and leaves 1866 out.

Date of the revelation: the article gives 12 December 1838 (26 October by the lunar calendar) in the timeline and 26 October 1838 elsewhere; the profile gives it as 26 October of the lunar calendar and, in the origins section, 12 December in the solar one.

The article does not say how Tenrikyo's end of Sect Shinto designation came about; the 1945 event is inferred from 'between 1908 and 1945', and its second clause is the article's present-tense statement about separation. The editor may want to cut the 1945 event if that is too strong.

The Osashizu: the article says Izo Iburi delivered directions from 4 January 1887; the 1887 event pairs this with Nakayama's death (26 January 1887, lunar calendar). The 1887 event's month is not given for the death in the solar calendar.

Spread: the article gives no growth figures before 1974 and no dates for the foreign centres, so the faith map keeps to the article's 'in recent years' and gives them no year of founding beyond that. The map's years for overseas areas are the editor's to confirm.
Left out: the Mishima Shrine location of the revelation (no coordinates safe), the Kagura ritual's details, the Shuyoka seminary course, lists of notable followers beyond two names.
